Ecuador became the largest banana exporter in the world in the 1950s, and still is. The banana boom began around 1948, when disease and hurricanes hit plantations in Central America.

Under President Galo Plaza, the state built roads and gave credit to growers in the coastal lowlands. Unlike in the banana republics of Central America, much of the fruit was grown by local medium-sized farmers rather than foreign companies, though foreign firms handled the trade.

The boom drew migrants from the highlands to the coast and to Guayaquil, and paid for a period of stable democracy. It followed the collapse of cacao and came before oil. Bananas remain one of the main exports of Ecuador, alongside oil and shrimp.
